extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, newsroom managers, and journalism students (particularly those doing investigative reporting on sexual assault)
extracted.subtask_description: Practices and newsroom policies for reporting and editing investigative features about campus sexual assault, including verification, attribution, fact-checking, legal review, and how to balance sensitivity to victims with rigorous reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification and independent reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must pursue independent reporting paths rather than rely solely on a single source’s account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of independent paths include checking social media and fraternity membership rolls, examining employment records (e.g., aquatic center hires), interviewing potential witnesses or front-line staff, and finding documentary evidence; the report cites multiple missed avenues (social-media checks, roster comparisons, contacting classmates or employees) that could have exposed contradictions and avoided publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking derogatory information
rubrics_metrics.description: Any derogatory information about named or identifiable people should be checked with those subjects before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece criticizes Rolling Stone for agreeing not to contact three friends and for not providing detailed allegations to Phi Kappa Psi, showing that merely asking 'Can you comment?' is insufficient. Journalistic practice—and fairness—requires seeking the subjects’ side; doing so can produce exculpatory facts or new leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confronting subjects with detailed allegations (not just 'comment')
rubrics_metrics.description: When seeking a response, journalists should present the specific, derogatory details they intend to publish so subjects can respond fully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withholding details to avoid 'front-running' is sometimes defensible, but generally risky; giving subjects full details may prompt investigations or produce contradictions that change reporting decisions (the Phi Kappa Psi example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid undue deference to victims when verification is required
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance respect and trauma-informed treatment of survivors with the obligation to verify factual claims; do not let sensitivity become a substitute for reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survivor autonomy and non-retraumatization are important, but reporters must make clear the verification process needs (Kristen Lombardi example). If a source will not allow necessary verification, reporters should be prepared to walk away or rethink publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroborating survivor accounts with documentary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek documentary corroboration such as hospital records, 911 calls, texts/emails, phone records, security or cellphone video, or contemporaneous statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report recommends exhaustive searches for any available shred of corroboration (Bogdanich example). It notes FERPA limits but also exceptions and ways sources can authorize release of records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain inconsistencies and trauma-related memory issues to readers
rubrics_metrics.description: If accounts contain inconsistencies, journalists should report and explain them rather than glossing over or hiding them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trauma can impair memory; explain how that may affect contradictory details. Readers should be told when important corroboration is lacking or when elements come from a single source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on a single source for a high-stakes narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should not invest a publication’s reputation in a single, uncorroborated source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Rolling Stone case shows the danger of building a major investigation around one person’s account without sufficient independent verification or corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudonym use: rare, disclosed, and tightly governed
rubrics_metrics.description: Pseudonyms are 'inherently undesirable' and should be used rarely, only after robust discussion and with clear alternatives explored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of pseudonyms can mask reporting gaps and create trust problems; the report suggests banning them or severely restricting them and requiring formal review/approval when they are considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checking rigor and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact-checkers must thoroughly verify key factual claims and have the authority and obligation to escalate serious concerns to senior editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The checker did spend hours with the source but failed to forcefully escalate unresolved problems. Fact-checkers should be instructed to come to department heads or senior editors when they encounter reporting holes or questionable editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checker and editorial escalation procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms must have clear procedures requiring fact-checkers to escalate concerns and giving them 'muscle' to challenge editorial decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department heads should make it explicit that staff must raise problems; the checking chief said she instructs staff to escalate, but that did not happen in this case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution clarity and transparency to readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit in on-the-record copy about what was independently verified and who was or was not contacted; do not use misleading attributions to obscure gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The story used attributions that implied multiple confirmations when some lines derived only from the main source; the checker flagged this but editors accepted obfuscation. Readers should be able to tell when a quotation or assertion originates from the single source vs. independent interviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial supervision, debate, and red-team skepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors at all levels should surface, debate, and challenge tough questions about sourcing, methodology, and attribution rather than deferring to consensus or authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report found an environment where editors and experienced staff failed to surface or vigorously debate problems; newsrooms should encourage dissent and structured review of risky claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and retain reporting records (notes, audio, transcripts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep contemporaneous notes, audio recordings, and transcripts to support the reporting process and post-publication review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rolling Stone provided a 405-page record and audio; the report used those materials to evaluate reporting decisions. Good documentation aids internal review and legal defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal review but clarity about scope and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with potentially defamatory allegations should receive legal review, but editorial teams should know what was raised and what issues remain unresolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report notes an unclear record of what the in-house lawyer questioned; attorney-client privilege can limit disclosure, but teams should still track legal concerns and resolve them before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency with sources about the reporting process and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Make explicit to sources what the reporting process will involve, including the need to obtain documents, talk to others, and seek comments from accused parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kristen Lombardi's practice of prefacing interviews by explaining verification needs and giving survivors control over pace/time is cited as a model. If subjects are unwilling to accept those terms, be prepared to stop reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand legal/institutional frameworks (Title IX, Clery Act, VAWA, OCR guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists covering campus sexual assault should understand federal and institutional rules governing reporting, student privacy, and universities’ obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing Title IX, the Clery Act, the Department of Education's directives, and FERPA (including its exceptions) helps reporters analyze institutional responses and hold them to account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus journalism on institutional response when proving guilt is infeasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Where proving factual guilt is difficult, emphasize investigation of how institutions handled allegations and whether their responses met legal and ethical standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach can serve public interest, be easier to corroborate, and can persuade reluctant sources to participate; the report recommends analyzing systems rather than attempting to adjudicate criminal guilt via reporting alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use front-line and background sources to triangulate accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Interview front-line staff (counselors, residence staff), student activists, and others who may provide corroborating context or contemporaneous signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These sources often are more willing to talk and can provide early signals and context about campus culture and institutional handling of complaints.
